questions.stem: In an experiment testing whether caffeine affects reaction time, the independent variable is:
options: the time of day at which participants are tested
the age of the participants
whether participants consume caffeine
participants' reaction times
questions.explanation: The independent variable is the one the researcher manipulates, here caffeine. Reaction time is what is measured, so it is the dependent variable.

questions.stem: A researcher tests whether listening to music while studying affects how many words from a 20-word list are recalled. What is the dependent variable?
options: The type of music played to participants while they study
The length of the word list given to each of the participants
The number of words correctly recalled from the list
Whether or not participants listen to music while studying
questions.explanation: The dependent variable is what the researcher measures to see the effect of the independent variable, here recall. Listening to music or not is the independent variable, and list length is a controlled variable.

questions.stem: Which is the best hypothesis for an investigation into sleep and memory?
options: It is hypothesised that Year 12 students who sleep 8 hours will recall more words from a 20-word list than those who sleep 5 hours
It is hypothesised that sleep has some kind of effect on the memory of people of every age, in every country, all around the world
It is hypothesised that students who sleep more will be happier at school and will also get higher results in all of their subjects
It is hypothesised that the amount of sleep a student gets has a large influence on many different aspects of their wellbeing
questions.explanation: A good hypothesis is testable and states the population, the independent variable, the dependent variable and the predicted direction. The other statements are too vague to test, or include more than one dependent variable.

questions.stem: In psychological research, a controlled variable is:
options: a variable that has already affected the results apart from the IV
a variable held constant so that it does not affect the dependent variable
the group of participants who are not exposed to the independent variable at all
the variable that the researcher measures to see the effect of the IV
questions.explanation: A controlled variable is kept constant so that changes in the dependent variable can be attributed to the independent variable. It is not the same as a control group, which is a group of participants.

questions.stem: In a memory study, participants in the music condition were all tested in the morning and those in the silence condition were all tested in the afternoon. Time of testing is best described as:
options: a potential confounding variable, because it differed systematically between conditions
the independent variable, because the researcher chose the testing time for each group
a controlled variable, because every participant was tested at a scheduled time
the dependent variable, because it may have changed the number of words recalled
questions.explanation: Because time of day differed between conditions, any difference in recall could be due to it rather than to music, so it may confound the results. A controlled variable would have been kept the same for all participants.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes an extraneous variable from a confounding variable?
options: A confounding variable may affect the DV; an extraneous variable has affected the DV and offers another explanation for the results
An extraneous variable is one the researcher holds constant; a confounding variable is the variable that the researcher manipulates
An extraneous variable affects only the control group; a confounding variable affects only the experimental group in a study
An extraneous variable may affect the DV; a confounding variable has affected the DV and offers another explanation for the results
questions.explanation: An extraneous variable is any variable other than the IV that might affect the results and should be controlled or monitored. If it is not controlled and does affect the DV, it becomes a confounding variable, threatening internal validity.

questions.stem: In a within-subjects design:
options: participants are observed in their natural setting without any manipulation
each participant is exposed to every condition of the independent variable
each participant is exposed to only one condition of the independent variable
some independent variables are tested within and some between participants
questions.explanation: In a within-subjects design the same participants complete all conditions, so they act as their own comparison. Exposure to only one condition describes a between-subjects design.

questions.stem: What is a key limitation of a within-subjects design?
options: Differences between the people in each group may confound the results of the study
It requires far more participants than a between-subjects design to give useful, meaningful data
It cannot be used to measure a dependent variable that is quantitative in nature
Order effects, such as practice or fatigue, may influence results in later conditions
questions.explanation: Because participants complete every condition, earlier conditions can affect performance in later ones through practice, fatigue or boredom. Differences between groups of people are a limitation of between-subjects designs, which within-subjects designs avoid.

questions.stem: Researchers want to test whether learning the method of loci improves recall. Why would a between-subjects design be more suitable than a within-subjects design?
options: A between-subjects design needs fewer participants overall, so it is quicker and cheaper to run with a class
A between-subjects design always produces greater internal validity than a within-subjects design does
Once participants learn the technique they cannot unlearn it, so a later no-technique condition would be contaminated
A between-subjects design removes every difference between participants, so it controls all extraneous variables
questions.explanation: Learning a mnemonic is not reversible, so participants could not complete a genuine no-technique condition afterwards. Between-subjects designs do not remove participant differences; random allocation only spreads them across groups.

questions.stem: A study measures anxiety before and after an eight-week mindfulness course in one group, and at the same two times in a second group that does not do the course. This is:
options: a correlational study
a mixed design
a within-subjects design
a between-subjects design
questions.explanation: The comparison of before and after within each group is within-subjects, and the comparison between the course and no-course groups is between-subjects, so the study combines both. It manipulates a variable, so it is not correlational.

questions.stem: A researcher records hours of screen time and sleep quality for 200 adolescents without manipulating any variable. This methodology is:
options: a controlled experiment
a case study
a simulation
a correlational study
questions.explanation: A correlational study observes and records variables as they naturally occur to find relationships between them. A controlled experiment would require the researcher to manipulate screen time.

questions.stem: The screen time study finds that more screen time is associated with poorer sleep quality. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Screen time causes poorer sleep quality, because the two variables were measured in the same adolescents
Poor sleep quality causes higher screen time, because tired adolescents are less likely to do other things
The two variables cannot be related in any way, because neither variable was manipulated by the researcher
Screen time and sleep quality are related, but it cannot be concluded that screen time causes poorer sleep
questions.explanation: A correlational study can show that variables are associated but not which causes which, or whether a third variable is responsible. Variables can be related without being manipulated; manipulation is needed only to test cause and effect.

questions.stem: A student collates and analyses the findings of published studies on the gut–brain axis to answer a research question. Which methodology is this?
options: Fieldwork
Modelling
A case study
A literature review
questions.explanation: A literature review collates and analyses secondary data from other people's findings. Fieldwork involves observing and interacting with a selected environment beyond the classroom.

questions.stem: Random sampling means that:
options: the researcher selects people who are readily available to take part
the population is divided into subgroups that are sampled in proportion
participants volunteer for the study by responding to an advertisement
every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected
questions.explanation: In random sampling every member of the population has the same chance of selection, which helps the sample represent the population. Sampling subgroups in proportion is stratified sampling.

questions.stem: A school's senior students are 60% Year 11 and 40% Year 12. A researcher randomly selects 30 Year 11 and 20 Year 12 students. This is:
options: convenience sampling
random allocation
stratified sampling
self-selected sampling
questions.explanation: The population was divided into subgroups and each was sampled in the same proportion as in the population, which is stratified sampling. Random allocation refers to placing participants into conditions, not selecting them.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of random allocation in a controlled experiment?
options: To give each member of the population an equal chance of being selected to take part in the experiment
To divide the population into subgroups and select participants from each subgroup in proportion
To make sure that every participant experiences every condition of the independent variable in a different order
To give each participant an equal chance of being placed in any group, spreading participant differences evenly
questions.explanation: Random allocation assigns the sample to conditions so that participant characteristics are likely to be similar across groups. Giving the population an equal chance of selection is random sampling, a separate step.

questions.stem: Increasing the sample size in an investigation mainly helps by:
options: removing systematic errors caused by a poorly calibrated piece of equipment
guaranteeing that every measurement is accurate and close to the true value
making the results less precise, because more scores are spread out widely
reducing the effect of random errors and making results more representative
questions.explanation: A larger sample reduces the influence of random variation and is more likely to represent the population. Systematic errors shift every reading in the same direction, so more participants do not remove them.

questions.stem: In VCE Psychology, random errors mainly affect:
options: the accuracy of measurements
the ethics of the investigation
the hypothesis being tested
the precision of measurements
questions.explanation: Random errors cause unpredictable variation, spreading readings out and reducing precision. Systematic errors shift all readings in one direction and affect accuracy.

questions.stem: A stopwatch used to time participants' reactions always starts 0.2 seconds late. This is:
options: a systematic error, which affects the accuracy of the results
a random error, which affects the precision of the results
a personal error, which should be included in the analysis
an outlier, which should be removed from the results
questions.explanation: A consistent offset in the same direction every time is a systematic error, which shifts results away from the true value and so reduces accuracy. Repeating measurements with the same stopwatch would not fix it.

questions.stem: While entering data, a researcher types a participant's score as 85 instead of 58. This is:
options: a personal error, which should be corrected rather than analysed
a random error, which is reduced by calculating a mean score
a systematic error, which shifts every score in one direction
uncertainty, which is present in every psychological measure
questions.explanation: Mistakes and miscalculations are personal errors. The study design says they should not be included in the analysis; the error should be corrected or the measurement repeated. A random error is unpredictable variation in measurement, not a recording mistake.

questions.stem: Which statement about uncertainty in psychological research is correct?
options: Uncertainty arises only from personal errors, such as mistakes when recording data
Measuring psychological constructs, such as stress, reduces the degree of uncertainty
All measurements have some uncertainty, which can be reduced but not completely removed
Uncertainty is another word for error, so the two terms can be used interchangeably
questions.explanation: Every measurement has uncertainty, reflecting a lack of exact knowledge of the true value. The study design stresses that error and uncertainty are not synonyms, and psychological constructs tend to increase uncertainty.

questions.stem: A timing device known to produce a signal lasting exactly 250 ms is measured four times, giving 300, 301, 299 and 300 ms. These measurements are:
options: precise but not accurate
accurate but not precise
both accurate and precise
neither accurate nor precise
questions.explanation: The readings agree closely with one another, so they are precise, but they are all about 50 ms from the true value, so they are not accurate. This pattern suggests a systematic error.

questions.stem: Reproducibility refers to the closeness of agreement between results obtained:
options: when the measured value is compared with the true value of the quantity
when values within one set of measurements are compared with each other
under changed conditions, such as a different observer, method or location
under the same conditions, by the same observer over a short period of time
questions.explanation: Reproducibility concerns agreement when conditions change, such as a different researcher or location. Agreement under the same conditions over a short time is repeatability.

questions.stem: A psychological investigation is internally valid if it:
options: is repeated by the same researcher under the same conditions
investigates what it sets out or claims to investigate
has results that apply to similar people in other settings
produces measurements that agree closely with each other
questions.explanation: Internal validity is whether the investigation actually investigates what it claims to, considering its design, sampling, allocation and extraneous variables. Applying results to similar people elsewhere is external validity.

questions.stem: A study of coping strategies uses only first-year psychology students at one Melbourne university. Which aspect of the study is this sampling most likely to limit?
options: External validity, as the results may not apply to people who differ from the sample
Repeatability, as the same researcher could not run the study again under the same conditions
Precision, as students' scores will be more spread out than those of the general public
Accuracy, as students cannot give true answers about the coping strategies they use
questions.explanation: A narrow sample may not resemble the wider population, limiting how far the findings can be generalised, which is external validity. The study could still be repeated in the same way, so repeatability is not the main concern.

questions.stem: For the scores 4, 6, 6, 7 and 12, which correctly gives the mean, median and mode?
options: Mean 6, median 7, mode 6
Mean 7, median 6, mode 12
Mean 7, median 7, mode 6
Mean 7, median 6, mode 6
questions.explanation: The mean is 35 ÷ 5 = 7. The median is the middle score when ordered, 6, and the mode is the most frequent score, also 6. The high score of 12 pulls the mean above the median.

questions.stem: A group's mean anxiety score fell from 40 before treatment to 30 after treatment. What is the percentage change?
questions.explanation: Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (30 − 40) ÷ 40 × 100 = −25%. Dividing by the new value, 30, gives −33.3%, which is a common slip.

questions.stem: In a sleep study, 18 of 24 participants reported improved sleep after a sleep hygiene program. What percentage is this?
questions.explanation: 18 ÷ 24 × 100 = 75%. The 25% is the proportion who did not report improvement, and 133% comes from dividing the wrong way.

questions.stem: Standard deviation is a measure of:
options: the average of all the scores in the data set
how spread out the scores are around the mean
the score that occurs most often in the data
the middle score when the data are in order
questions.explanation: Standard deviation describes variability: a small value means scores cluster close to the mean, and a large value means they are spread out. The most common score is the mode, and the middle score is the median.

questions.stem: Two groups have the same mean memory score. Group X has a standard deviation of 2 and Group Y has a standard deviation of 9. What does this show?
options: Group X's scores are less precise than the scores of Group Y
Group X must contain more outliers than Group Y contains
Group Y's scores are more spread out around the mean than Group X's
Group Y's scores are higher overall than the scores of Group X
questions.explanation: A larger standard deviation means greater variability, so Group Y's scores are spread more widely. Because the means are equal, neither group scored higher overall.

questions.stem: In a reaction time study, one participant's time is 2900 ms, while all other times are between 250 and 400 ms. What should the researcher do?
options: Investigate the outlier, such as checking for a recording error, before deciding how to treat it
Delete the outlier straight away, because results that are unusual are always caused by mistakes
Ignore the outlier, because a single extreme value cannot have any effect on the group's mean
Replace the outlier with the group's highest normal result so that the mean is less affected
questions.explanation: The study design states that outliers must be analysed and accounted for rather than automatically dismissed; they may be genuine or caused by error. A single extreme value can strongly affect the mean.

questions.stem: On a graph of results, the independent variable is plotted on:
options: the vertical axis
a separate key
the graph's title only
the horizontal axis
questions.explanation: By convention the independent variable goes on the horizontal (x) axis and the dependent variable on the vertical (y) axis.

questions.stem: Which type of graph is most suitable for presenting mean recall scores for three separate conditions: music, white noise and silence?
options: A frequency table
A bar chart
A line graph
A pie chart
questions.explanation: When the independent variable is made up of separate categories, a bar chart is used. A line graph suits an independent variable that is continuous, such as hours of sleep.

questions.stem: Which ethical guideline ensures that participants can stop taking part in a study at any time without penalty?
options: Confidentiality
Debriefing
Withdrawal rights
Voluntary participation
questions.explanation: Withdrawal rights allow participants to discontinue at any time, during or after the study, and to have their results removed. Voluntary participation is about freely choosing to take part in the first place, without coercion.

questions.stem: A researcher tells participants a study is about attention when it actually measures conformity. Under the study design's guidelines, this use of deception is acceptable only if:
options: participants are paid for their time, and the results of the study are kept strictly confidential afterwards
the study is going to be published, and the researcher has many years of experience
participants are under 18, and a parent or guardian has given written consent
knowing the true purpose would change participants' behaviour, and they are debriefed afterwards
questions.explanation: Deception is permitted only when knowing the true aim would affect participants' behaviour and the validity of the study, and debriefing is then essential. Payment, publication or parental consent do not justify deception.

questions.stem: Which ethical concept is the commitment to maximising benefits and minimising the risks and harms of a course of action?
options: Non-maleficence
Justice
Integrity
Beneficence
questions.explanation: Beneficence is about maximising benefits while minimising risks and harms. Non-maleficence is about avoiding harm, or at least ensuring any harm is not disproportionate to the benefits.

questions.stem: A researcher reports all of her results honestly, including those that do not support her hypothesis. Which ethical concept does this best reflect?
options: Justice
Integrity
Beneficence
Respect
questions.explanation: Integrity involves honest reporting of all sources and results, whether favourable or unfavourable, so they can be scrutinised. Beneficence concerns maximising benefits and minimising harm.

questions.stem: A new therapy for phobia is tested on volunteers from many backgrounds, but afterwards only people who can afford high fees will have access to it. Which ethical concept is most at issue?
options: Confidentiality
Justice
Integrity
Beneficence
questions.explanation: Justice requires a fair distribution of, and access to, the benefits of an action, with no unfair burden on any group. Here the benefits would go only to those who can pay. Confidentiality is an ethical guideline about personal information, not a concept about fairness.

questions.stem: For a 15-year-old to take part in a psychology experiment at school, informed consent should be obtained from:
options: the student's class teacher
the school's principal alone
the student's closest friend
a parent or legal guardian
questions.explanation: The study design states that if participants are unable to give consent themselves, a parent or legal guardian should provide it, which applies to participants under 18. A teacher or principal cannot consent on a student's behalf.

questions.stem: Before running a study in which participants stay up late, a student completes a risk assessment. Its main purpose is to:
options: identify potential hazards to participants and plan ways to reduce them
increase the internal validity of the results that the study produces
record each participant's written consent before the study begins
replace the need for debriefing participants after the study ends
questions.explanation: A risk assessment identifies hazards, such as fatigue or travelling home tired, and sets out how they will be managed. Consent and debriefing are separate ethical requirements that a risk assessment does not replace.

questions.stem: Which statement is evidence rather than anecdote or opinion?
options: A controlled experiment with 120 participants found that restricted sleep reduced recall
My uncle says he works much better on four hours' sleep than he ever did on eight hours
A well-known sportsperson says that mindfulness meditation completely changed her life
Many people believe that teenagers stay up late mainly because they are being lazy
questions.explanation: Evidence comes from systematically collected data, such as a controlled experiment. A personal story is anecdote, and a belief held by many people is opinion, however common it is.

questions.stem: A student's results show a difference in the predicted direction, but there were only 8 participants, all from her own class. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
options: The results can be generalised to all adolescents, because the participants were adolescents
The results support the hypothesis, but the small, unrepresentative sample limits generalisation
The results prove the hypothesis, because the difference was in the direction that was predicted
The results refute the hypothesis, because a sample of 8 can never produce any useful data
questions.explanation: Data can support or fail to support a hypothesis but never prove it. A small, non-representative sample increases uncertainty and limits external validity, which should be identified as a limitation of the conclusion.

questions.stem: Which statement about psychological models, such as the Atkinson-Shiffrin multi-store model, is most accurate?
options: Models are exact copies of brain structures, so they show precisely where memory is stored
A model must be discarded completely as soon as any single limitation of it is identified
Models are personal opinions, so they cannot be tested against evidence from research
Models organise and explain observations, but they simplify reality and have limitations
questions.explanation: Models are simplified representations used to organise and understand phenomena and to make testable predictions. All models have limitations, and they are refined or replaced as evidence accumulates rather than discarded at the first problem.

questions.stem: A memory test written in the United States includes items about baseball. It is used to compare the memory of Australian and American students. What is the main problem?
options: The test will measure memory accurately in both groups, because memory does not vary between people
The test will reduce random error, because students from both countries take exactly the same items
The unfamiliar content may disadvantage Australian students, so the results reflect cultural bias rather than memory
The test will be more precise for Australian students, because the items are new to them and so are harder for them to answer
questions.explanation: Items that depend on cultural familiarity mean differences in scores may reflect background knowledge rather than memory, so the measure lacks validity for comparing these groups. The study design asks students to consider cultural biases in data and conclusions.

questions.stem: In a VCE Psychology scientific poster, the communication statement is:
options: a section introducing new information that was not presented in the results section
a one-sentence summary of the key finding that answers the investigation question
the list of references and acknowledgements for sources used in the investigation
a brief outline of the methodology and the data generation methods that were used
questions.explanation: The communication statement sits at the centre of the poster and reports the key finding in one sentence. The conclusion, like the rest of the poster, should not introduce new information.
